title.en: Language work for Winds of Change: fixed word pairs, collocations, present perfect tense and art words

text.en: In Winds of Change, skilled artisans turn bamboo, thread and silk into traditional hand fans called pankhas, while Canvas of Soil paints a garden in vivid brushstrokes. Notice how certain English words always travel together in a fixed order.

keepEnglishTerms: Links past action to present relevance

text.en:
Unit 3 pairs descriptive words from the essay by meaning: appearance pairs such as exotic and stylish or ornate and encrusted, place pairs such as villages and towns or within and outside, and material pairs such as thread and wool or silk and brass.
Many common expressions joined by 'and' follow a fixed order that cannot be reversed, often placing the shorter word first—for example bread and butter, never butter and bread.
Learn eight fixed expressions from the unit table: high and dry means stranded without help or money, cut and run means make a sudden escape, and all and sundry means everyone rather than a select few.
Check the remaining fixed pairs: facts and figures gives accurate detailed information, wear and tear names damage from ordinary use, thick and thin means through all difficulties, time and again means often, and hard and fast means fixed without exception.
Word combinations that naturally sound right together are called collocations—such as sustainable livelihood, aesthetically pleasing, and appreciating the culture in this chapter.
Practise everyday verb collocations accurately: students take an exam (never give an exam when writing it as a student), candidates take or have a seat, and scooters run into cars.
Two more key collocations appear in the exercise: we say take responsibility for our success, and we say improve my grammar rather than tone up grammar.
Now study the verb form in: 'In modern times, pankhas have become traditional craft items' and 'this handicraft has transformed into a commercial business'. That structure is the present perfect tense.
Present perfect tense links a completed past action or change to its relevance right now in the present—formed with have or has followed by the third form (past participle) of the verb.
Applying the rule to the puppetry paragraph: 'Puppeteers have created intricate characters', 'They have mastered delicate movements', 'puppetry has evolved', 'have passed down their craft', and 'They have performed in theatres'.
In the poem Canvas of Soil, colour vocabulary expands from basic red, green and blue to rich shades: scarlet, crimson, vermilion and salmon for red; jade, olive and pistachio for green; indigo, cobalt and denim for blue.
Notice also how writers use studio terms in context—easel holds the wooden frame, canvas receives the paint, portrait depicts a person's face, and palette mixes the hues.
For the Unit 3 listening dialogue between Rohan and Priya, listen for reasons why a bamboo or mirror-work pankha suits Grandma's verandah evenings and why consulting their mother matters.
When writing your two-to-three-paragraph descriptive piece in Unit 3, weave accurate colour shades, sensory verbs, and natural collocations into an organised summary of the scene.

problem.en: Rewrite the collocation mistakes and complete the tense blank: (a) Students must give their science test carefully. (b) Over the years, puppetry ___ (evolve) using modern staging.

text.en: (a) Replace 'give their science test' with 'take their science test'.

why.en: In English collocation, teachers set or give a test, while students take or sit an exam.
'Puppetry' is singular uncountable, so it takes 'has' plus the past participle 'evolved' to connect past growth to the present.

prompt.en: Explain what collocations and fixed 'and' expressions are, and tell how present perfect tense connects past to present.

requiredIdeas.en: Fixed 'and' expressions keep an irreversible order (e.g., high and dry, all and sundry)
Collocations are natural conventional combinations like take an exam or improve grammar
Present perfect uses has/have + past participle for past events relevant now

commonMisconceptions.en: Writing butter and bread or say students give an exam
Using simple past instead of has/have + past participle for ongoing present impact

points.en: Fixed expressions with 'and' keep a set order: high and dry, cut and run, facts and figures, wear and tear, thick and thin.
Collocations are natural word partners: take an exam, take a seat, take responsibility, improve grammar.
Present perfect tense (has/have + past participle) links past events or developments to the present.
Colour and studio terms like vermilion, pistachio, indigo, easel, palette and canvas sharpen descriptive writing.
